en: Preface:

Since the dawn of the land of China, when the potential of the Han court was first awakened, a great sage emerged to follow the path of destiny. The *palm-leaf* scriptures arrived in abundance through successive translations;

thus, the Four Reliances appeared. Out of compassion for those in the five turbidities, they repeatedly beat the Dharma drum of the three voids, causing the Great Truth of the One Ultimate to resound far and wide.
The Zongleng [Commentary]: Those lost on the path find a guide to follow; those who practice see the road to awakening opened wide.
For this reason, the Patriarch Xianshou established his teachings based on the Perfect and Sudden (Dharmalakṣaṇa), providing commentaries for all the various scriptures without exception.

The Venerable Tiantai upheld the refutation of heterodox views to provide the guiding framework, hanging high the golden mirror to sweep away lingering dust. Yet, as the ages have grown distant and people have declined, these subtle words...
Consequently, it fell into decline. Lacking the substance of a true sage, we merely possessed the empty prestige of being lecturers;

thus, when encountering the dust of worldly affairs, we were utterly without a basis for reliance, leaving those who carry their books upon bamboo frames with nowhere to turn. Fortunately, our former teacher arose, causing the fortunes of the Dharma to flourish once more.

He inherited the noble counsel of his predecessors and opened wide the eye of wisdom that encompasses all life. Only then did the natures and characteristics [of phenomena] begin to be distinguished without confusion.
At this point, the traditions of Tiantai and Xuanzang diverged. However, while the *Lotus Sūtra* has been widely circulated, it uniquely lacked commentaries from its own school.

Therefore, I have returned to the original intent of the Śākya Buddha’s descent into the world and re-examined the universal principles and fundamental sources of the Buddhas’ preaching of the Dharma.

Having already clarified the essential purport of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in my *Great Commentary*, I have now adopted its principles to judge this sūtra, so that its great outlines may be fully revealed.

Who would say that the *Kōki* contains only the meaning of the "Half-Essence" (*han-i*)? Alas! I intended to propagate and expound its broad meaning, yet who could have foreseen that my life would suddenly be transmitted as a mere record of the truth?
For forty years it has lain in silence; how can one speak of the hundreds of thousands of traces of his own hand? Within my mouth, I can only sigh in admiration of his exemplary conduct.

Alas, I am unfortunate; I entered the gate of this school too late. In my coming and going, I have been nearly intimate with the person of the Master and have attended his lecture hall on four occasions.

It is not only that my learning and experience are meager, but my ignorance and incompetence are also extreme. Nevertheless, as I stand at the edge of the Dharma altar, how could I forget the debt of gratitude owed to the "wood-root" (the teacher)?

Whenever I regard the Master’s bequeathed writings, I lament that they remain incomplete, like shards of jade yet to be joined. Undaunted by my own triviality and obscurity, I have ventured to compose this supplement.

Diao regrets that my exposition of the meaning is unrefined; I have merely incurred the reproach of being smeared with dung, and my pen has faltered in its resonance, truly lacking the sound of vibrating jade.
To have been erroneously granted this initial rank in the treasury of jewels was to act as the first instigator for those like us; the guilt is difficult to evade.

As for merit, there is truly none. I pray that the wise and eminent may extensively revise and edit it, ensuring that it assists the teaching without contradiction and that it accords with the established categories.
Thus it is recorded in the appended chapter.

The Śramaṇa Fuxian of Western Shu exhorted the Great Master; his disciple Zhii Xuedun established the topical outline.
We, the compilers of the *Shiyi*, prostrate ourselves before the Unsurpassed Honored One, the Lotus Sūtra, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra.
Śāriputra, Kāśyapa, and the others—through my own meager and inferior wisdom—I shall now explain this profound and solid treasury.
May the merit and benefit of turning back [the flow of ignorance] cause all beings to universally receive the Honored One’s prediction [of enlightenment].
To explain this sutra, I shall first provide a preliminary exposition of its thematic gates and then offer a word-by-word commentary; in total, there are seven sections.

1. The causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; 2. The classification and inclusion within the *piṭakas* and vehicles (*yāna*); 3. The delimitation of the principles and meanings; 4. The essence of the teaching as the expressive medium; 5.
The fundamental purport and its application to specific capacities; 6. A general explanation of the title; 7. A detailed interpretation of the text and its meaning. Question:
Generally, those who follow the school of Xuanzhuo (Xianshou) employ ten gates when commenting on a sūtra. Why are there only seven here? Answer: Observe that...

When the Patriarch [Zhiyan] was annotating the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he encountered every single word and phrase as an occasion to connect it to the ten directions, thereby manifesting the inexhaustibility of the distinct principal and attendant teachings.
Consequently, within his commentary, he employed the "perfect numbers" (*yuan-shu*) to align with the original scripture, establishing the principle of connecting to the inexhaustible.
This is its unique significance. Generally, when one composes a work, if one does not...
Please examine the *Heart Sūtra* and the two commentaries on the *Awakening of Faith* by the Patriarch [Tiantai] with leisure and profound care;
their intent will then become clear. First, regarding the causes and conditions: when sages establish their teachings, there must be a specific purpose.
Just as Mount Sumeru and the vast ocean are only moved by great causes, so too do we now shake the mountain of the Tathāgata’s refined golden virtue and stir his deep and expansive wisdom.

The ocean is not a matter of minor cause. Thus, the Sūtra says: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great causal event (mahā-kāraṇa), namely, to open, reveal, awaken, and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Now, regarding this great causal event, each shall be opened into seven meanings; their general outline will be briefly indicated. As for the number seven, it is to accord with the seven axes and the seven [turns].

Regarding the meaning of the metaphors, there are seven prior causes: first, because it is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); second, to repay past causes; third, to accord with the resonance of the faculties;
fourth, to cause the branches to return to the root; fifth, to reveal the causal nature; sixth, to manifest the merit of the fruit;
and seventh, to benefit those of the present and future. Regarding the first point, "the nature of phenomena": the sagely wisdom perceives afar across the ten realms.

To summarize: although the specific events may not have occurred exactly as described, the fundamental distinction between the beginning and the end has already been established. Therefore, as one follows the momentum of various capacities and adapts to them, the teachings vary accordingly.
Thus, our World-Honored One, steering the wheel of great vows, manifested his body within the five turbidities and employed ten modes of conduct and five methods of teaching.
May it extend universally to all, so that they may together ascend the shore of enlightenment.

Yet, alas, there is another class of beings whose capacities are such that, although they initially entered the assembly of the fundamental One Vehicle Dharma, they remain as if deaf and blind, possessing no hearing or sight whatsoever.

Therefore, World-Honored One, from the beginning down to the end, you first used the three vehicles to attract and gather [beings], waiting until they had reached maturity before using the single vehicle that destroys distinctions to open their knowledge and vision, leading them to enter the Buddha-wisdom. Thus, a sutra says:
"These sentient beings should, by means of this Dharma, gradually attain entry into the Way. It further says: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, desire to cause sentient beings..."
"Opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision so that it may be made pure," and "appearing in the world," and so forth—all such phrases have the meaning of *dharmatā* (the natural order of things).
Second, regarding "repaying past causes": the opening of the Dharma's course arises from the profound cultivation of former lives.

If one realizes the ultimate identity of the Buddha-nature, one naturally takes pity on the masses who are suddenly deluded by difference. Without relying on those who have already awakened, how could later beings be rescued?
Kun. Thus, through the flowing forth of great compassion, he skillfully provides guidance to repay his past causes. Although these past causes are manifold, they do not exceed two types:
aspiration and practice. First, regarding the power of aspiration, the Sūtra says: "As I have previously vowed, that vow is now fulfilled;
I shall transform all sentient beings and cause them all to enter the Buddha-way. This refers precisely to the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra.
This is merely to fulfill my long-cherished vow. Regarding the power of practice, the Sūtra says:

"The Buddha-way that I have practiced, I desire that all sentient beings may likewise attain this Way. It further says: "Therefore, I became a great king and diligently sought until I obtained this Dharma."
Thus, he ultimately attained Buddhahood; I now speak for your sake because all that is spoken here is a recompense for past practices.
Third, regarding responding to the resonance of capacity: the Sage has no fixed response, yet he manifests in accordance with sincere devotion. Although it is said that the response arises from...

When there is a stimulus, there must be a response; for the essence [of the Buddha] must first possess a kind of supreme function that accords with conditions (*pratyaya*) before it can avoid rendering the叩 (stimulus) in vain.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "The Buddha, knowing their mental activities, teaches them the Mahāyāna. This demonstrates that teaching them is precisely in accordance with the nature of their stimulus.

Regarding "bringing the branches back to the root": this means that the gathering of the branches depends upon the extension of those branches; yet for there to be an extension of branches, there must necessarily be a root capable of extending them.

The *Five Classics* state: "First they see my body and hear what I preach. This specifically refers to the fact that in the past, [the Buddha] preached the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as the fundamental teaching.
Subsequently, for those who had not yet understood, he used the "One Vehicle of the Identical Teaching" (*tóngjiào yīshèng*) to harmonize with the ultimate reality.

This is for the sake of expedient means; by teaching the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, one tames those of inferior faculties until they reach the stage of maturity, and then leads them into the Buddha-wisdom.
Thus, this present sutra itself possesses the power to subsume the derivative aspects and draw forth its own essence to serve as the direct cause.

The merit of its final dissemination likewise belongs to the provisional teaching (*tongjiao*). If one were to discuss the power and function of this sutra comprehensively, there should be two aspects.

First, in relation to what precedes it, it is able to subsume those sentient beings who were the objects of the provisional, branch-level wheel of Dharma from the past, causing them to become like oneself by enabling them to hear this sutra.
Second, in relation to what follows, because it has subsumed the branches through itself, it immediately conceals [the provisional].

One’s own power and that which was initially entered are both what is induced; following that which can equally induce entry into the Buddha-wisdom of the *Avataṃsaka*, this is precisely returning to the fundamental power.
Question: Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* itself possesses Buddha-wisdom, why point so far back [to the *Avataṃsaka*]?
Answer: This Buddha-wisdom and that Buddha-wisdom are fundamentally not two different things. As the sutra says: "I now also cause them to enter."
The meaning of the Buddha’s wisdom-words is that they clarify how one follows from the latter back to the former, just like travelers on a road:
there has never been one who arrives at the destination last without following the guide who came before. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka* is like the great ocean, capable of receiving all streams.
Furthermore, this sutra is like the great ocean’s mouth: it can encompass all streams and enable them to have a place of return, achieving a supreme and vast efficacy.
Regarding the five causes for the nature of opening: these refer to what the sutra describes as the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, as well as his vast lifespan.

All these are based on the fact that the nature of sentient beings is inherently complete from the beginning. If one’s nature were not like gold or jade, then even with carving, it could not become a precious vessel.

It is precisely because sentient beings take the virtue of their nature as their substance and rely on the ocean of wisdom as their source, yet their forms change and their substance becomes distinct, and their emotions arise such that wisdom is obstructed.
Now, we cause them to know that the mind merges with the substance and to realize the fundamental while forgetting emotions; therefore, this is discussed.
The Sūtra provides a demonstration, stating that all phenomena possess such a nature, such characteristics, and so forth; therefore, they must be revealed.
The meaning of this revelation shall be explained in detail within the subsequent section on the teaching of the Dharma.

Sixth, regarding the manifestation of the merit of the fruit: since ordinary sentiments are not yet exhausted, the realm of the sages is difficult to fathom. Upon encountering something extraordinary, one is left bewildered and at a loss.

Thus, within a single *kṣaṇa*, one marvels that what took eight years to achieve has been accomplished; yet in Gayā, one remains ignorant of how long it has been since the distant realization was attained.
Without receiving the Sage’s instruction, how could one understand the profound mysteries? How much more so when the Prince himself provides a re-exposition!
When Dīpaṃkara received his prediction, was it not already a direct overturning of the remote root? Therefore, those who emerged from the earth were mostly elders;
truly, the father was young while the sons were old. It is no wonder that even the One Who Occupies the Place of Succession (the Bodhisattva Maitreya) remained deluded.

Only upon hearing the teaching on the vast measure of his lifespan did he realize that the merit of the fruition is inconceivable. Those who received this benefit were so numerous that they attained swift realization in a single lifetime.
Regarding "unsurpassed": it is calculated by means of the number of atoms in one set of four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*), thereby causing the assembly to resolve to emulate [the Buddha].

Regarding "seven benefits for the future": this refers to all sentient beings; since they equally possess the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*), [they shall likewise possess] the Buddha’s lifespan.

Therefore, its benefits will extensively reach the infinite realms of the present and the future. Those who hear this teaching while the Dharma assembly is still in session have already gained benefit;

furthermore, all those after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa who see or hear even a single verse or a single line of this complete sutra shall enter the light of the Tathāgata’s prophetic record—all of which is brought about by the power of this sutra.
The second [section] clarifies the conditions for the preaching of the sūtras. This refers to the time, place, persons, and so forth mentioned at the beginning of all sūtras;
these are all "conditions" (*pratyaya*). There are also seven types: first, based on time; second, based on place; third, based on the principal [teacher];
fourth, based on samādhi; fifth, based on manifested signs; sixth, based on the requester; and seventh, based on the listeners.
First: Now, the Sage is fundamentally unborn; thus, he should bring about a sublime assembly that will surely be of great benefit.
Only when the conditions for both self and others have matured does he then mount the occasion to inaugurate his mission, so that all living beings may hasten toward him.

Therefore, Mahāvīra sat in silent meditation for ten great kalpas, and our Buddha contemplated for twenty-one days; both were waiting for the proper time. When the time arrived, the teaching arose—not by mere chance.
Therefore it is said: "The reason I have not yet spoken is that the time for speaking has not yet arrived. It is also said: "Now is precisely that time;

I shall definitively expound the Mahāyāna," and so forth. Question: Since the true text is not obscured and the numinous realm eternally persists, when Great Master Zhiyi attained the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra, he saw the assembly on Vulture Peak as solemnly present as ever, without having dispersed. Why, then, was this [expounding] further initiated?

Feyi replied: "This is indeed a sign of profound faith and understanding. As for the single descent from the palace of Śuddhodana and the three circumambulations of Vulture Peak, these belong to the completion of the Buddha’s own mission; they are not comparable to this."
Regarding the second basis: when one realizes the ultimate limit of reality, both subject and object vanish together;

yet when one looks down to respond to the various capacities of sentient beings, the environment and its inhabitants appear distinctly. Whether termed "defiled" or "pure," or "self" or "other," these are all the elegant norms for engaging with the world.
This is the skillful means for delivering sentient beings. Why is this so? Without manifesting a physical body, there would be no way to gather those who aspire to return;
without adorning the land, there would be no way to provide rest for those on their path toward it.

Therefore, one must control and master the numinous realm before one can entrust one’s traces there and delight the spirit. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have always been on Vulture Peak."
...and so forth. This clarifies the locus of reliance. Question: The Great Sūtra states that the Buddha’s body fills the entire Dharma-realm;
why then do you say he is always present on Vulture Peak? Answer: Have you not seen that the second line of this very verse says, "He manifests universally before all multitudes"?
Furthermore, one must understand that although the Buddha’s body pervades the Dharma-realm, his gathering of sentient beings through skillful means is always at this mountain. For instance:
This land, Mount Qingliang, because of its Great Faith Vulture Peak, is already considered the foremost among the three thousand worlds;

how much more so now that it truly belongs to the Buddha-land? Furthermore, it may serve as a demonstration of a definitive direction for those who have not yet been able to directly understand "mind-only.
Question: Regarding the place where this sutra is currently being preached, is it defiled or pure? Answer: From the perspective of the Buddha, [it is pure].
In terms of verbal expression, the superior and the inferior are equal; yet when they manifest according to the capacities of beings, the defiled and the pure are distinguished. As the Sūtra says:

"Sentient beings see the end of the kalpa, while [others] see it as always filled with devas and humans," and so forth. It is also like the six realms of existence, where all alike see the same water.

One must know that only those who have forgotten the views of defilement and purity can fully perceive both defilement and purity; whereas those who remain within the states of defilement and purity...

They are unable to see each other’s realms. I privately maintain that, regardless of whether one belongs to the Great or Small Vehicle, prior to attaining the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (transformation body), the lands perceived by them are generally seen in accordance with the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of their respective dwellings.

Thus, what is seen by those with the three faculties is likewise the same five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*); for the Noble Path can only extinguish afflictions (*kleśa*), but cannot extinguish karmic retribution (*vipāka*).

Therefore, one must further understand that the three transformations of the pure land do not merely await the arrival of a Buddha to respond to the capacities of beings. To discuss this comprehensively, there are four possible permutations regarding what is perceived:
first, perceiving only the defiled, which is what is seen by those of both the Great and Lesser Vehicles who have not yet transcended the realm of birth and death (*pariccheda-śarīra*);
second, perceiving only the pure, which is what is seen by those of both the Great and Lesser Vehicles who have already attained the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).

Regarding "those who see": third, the simultaneous presence of both defilement and purity; this refers to the Buddha’s response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which appears in accordance with the capacities of beings within lands that they perceive as identical.
Fourth, the simultaneous cessation of both; this is spoken from the perspective of the Buddha’s own intrinsic state, because the characteristics of defilement and purity have been exhausted.

Furthermore, the first two phrases are stated provisionally based on those who follow the provisional teachings and have neither yet turned their minds nor entered the ultimate reality. As for those who have already entered the stage of the right-determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*): [they...]
One attains a partial conformity with what the Buddha perceives because one is able to know that phenomena are like illusions. Nevertheless, there are two types.
For those who have not yet severed their fetters (*saṃyojana*), they attain conformity with the Buddha’s vision at the time of entering meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*).

For those who have already severed the active afflictions (*kleśa*), they may partially conform to the Buddha’s vision regardless of whether they are emerging from or entering meditative observation. Furthermore, there are four cases (*catuṣkoṭi*).
1. Only defiled: this refers to the Sahā world, because it obscures the pure aspect. 2. Only pure: this refers to what is seen after the three transformations. 3. Both defiled and pure:
this refers to seeing the great ocean and the dragon maiden within the sites of the three transformations. 4. Neither defiled nor pure:
this refers to the *dharmatā*-land, wherein even purity does not exist; how much less could one speak of impurity? If [the text] were to continue...
Speaking specifically of Vulture Peak Mountain alone, there should further be four permutations regarding the universal and the particular: 1. Only particular:

This refers to what is seen by those who possess the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). 2. Only universal: This refers to the Buddha’s constant retinue, who are able to know that this very place is the nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
3. Both particular and universal: This refers to a single individual, at a time when they have not yet attained realization and...
Once this has been understood, because what is perceived may be either broad or narrow, there are four cases that are neither universal nor restricted;

this is because essence and appearance are fundamentally interpenetrating. If one further discusses this in terms of formation and destruction, there should likewise be another four cases, which can be understood through reflection; thus, there are sixteen cases in total.
Third, regarding the "Dependent on the Master" (yishou): The True Body has no body, and its wondrous marks have no marks.

It is like the fundamental purity of a mani-jewel, resembling a spiritual mirror that contains all reflections. Thus, it may be seen differently by different beings simultaneously, with their respective superior or inferior qualities clearly manifest;

or, following conditions in succession, it may be seen differently in various places. Therefore, what is presented and what is perceived all arise from the capacity for understanding of the sentient beings.

[Regarding] the ritual protocol: if one intends to emulate the Great Sage, one should speak in this manner. Now, in preaching this sutra, the Buddha himself should, according to the capacities of sentient beings, determine his physical form and distinguish the teachings through that manifested body;

thus, from the beginning, there shall be no error or discrepancy. If one considers the sequence from the first to the last of the eight phases [of a Buddha's life], it should properly be categorized as a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya).

If we discuss this according to principle, although it does not constitute the complete ten bodies (*daśakāya*), it is nonetheless a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*) in which the true body and the responsive body are mutually integrated, manifesting the three bodies in their perfection.

Generally speaking, among the various sūtras that adapt to the capacities of sentient beings, those that are "small" are small from beginning to end—such as the transformation Buddhas perceived in the *Caturāgama* and similar texts;
whereas those that are "great" are definitively great from beginning to end—such as the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
Regarding the Buddhas perceived by [the disciples of] the various [Hīnayāna] schools, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* alone stands in stark contrast to all other teachings.
Prior to its opening and elucidation—from the beginning at Rṣipatana until the summit of Vulture Peak—what was perceived therein was no less than as different as heaven and earth.

As the Sūtra says, "He immediately cast off his jeweled necklace and put on coarse, tattered garments"; this principle of concealing the superior and manifesting the inferior is expressed by the word "cast off."

It was merely a matter of changing from wearing tattered rags. When one’s knowledge and vision are opened and the time for receiving the prophecy arrives, the elder who entrusts the family estate remains none other than that former self who wore the tattered rags; yet, there is no text whatsoever stating that he sheds the tattered rags and puts on new ones.
Because at the moment the Dharma-eye becomes clear and bright, one immediately perceives the non-obstruction between the Real and the Responsive—where else could there be [such a change]?
Is there not a deluded and flowery interpretation here? Therefore, the Sūtra says: "This Dharma abides in the station of Dharma; the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.
If even the characteristics of the world can be eternally abiding, how much more so the Buddha-body? Furthermore, it says: "By means of the thirty-two marks, one adorns the Dharmakāya.
Is this not a reference to the true and responsive [bodies] being fused as one? Nevertheless, when distinguishing the three bodies, there must necessarily be...
Four propositions: First, the transformation body is not the true [body]. This refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha of the eight manifestations. As the sutra says:
"All say that the present Śākyamuni Buddha left the palace of the Śākyas and went not far from the city of Gayā," and so forth. Second, the true [body] is not the transformation body.
This refers to that which dwells in the *dharmatākāya* within the *dharmatābhūmi*. As the sutra says: "There is no birth-and-death, neither falling back nor..."

The first three [categories] are both real and transformational; these refer to the bodies of the mutual identity of the Real and the Responsive (True and Apparitional) perceived after one has attained understanding.
The fourth is neither real nor transformational. As the Sūtra says: "From afar he saw the elder, within his gate, providing a great jeweled canopy."
"Sitting upon the lion throne" refers to the term for the Supreme Response-Body (Sambhogakāya).

Regarding "the fourth [point], relying on samādhi": this means that when a noble one (*ārya*) preaches the Dharma, they must first enter into meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). Briefly, there are three meanings:
first, to demonstrate the model to future disciples, making it clear that a teaching is about to be given; second, to calmly contemplate the preceding principles so that the recipients may...
The intent is earnest. Sentient beings have long been obscured by the dust of afflictions;

were it not for the prior reception of correct meditative attainment (*samyag-samādhi*) and the secret empowerment that enables them to hear this, how could they profoundly accord with the true source and cut off the flow of delusion?

Therefore, the words spoken after attaining concentration can cause the net of doubt to be severed as easily as slicing through wood with a blade. Question: Upon which samādhi does the preaching of this sutra now rely? Is it the "Victorious" (*Vijaya*) or the "Superior" (*Abhyudgata*)? Answer:
There are two interpretations. One states that the Great Commentary identifies this as the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings; another states it is the Lotus Samādhi.

This means that since this single sutra takes the refutation of heterodoxy as its primary tenet, and what is now being expounded is the wondrous Dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), the samādhi upon which it relies must necessarily be the wondrous samādhi of the true mark wherein the one suchness is manifested. How, then, could there be any doubt?
Therefore, those who attain this samādhi will see the single assembly on Vulture Peak as solemnly present and undispersed.
Although this sutra contains no explicit text regarding entering meditative concentration, when reasoning is drawn from the facts, there is nothing else upon which to rely but this.
Question: Since the World-Honored One has already emerged from meditative absorption to preach the sūtra, how do we know that he enters it again? Answer:

The Sage of the Ultimate Fruit has already transcended all agitation and movement. Those who perceive him as entering and emerging do so merely for the sake of responding to the capacities of sentient beings;
how much more so when his entry and emergence are unimpeded, and movement and stillness share a single source?

Fifth, regarding the manifestation of signs: the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is tranquil and void, fundamentally devoid of all marks. Yet these marks of the markless do not obstruct the profusion of activity;
thus, the establishment of the teaching takes many forms, and its manifestations are not uniform. Sometimes light is emitted and the earth shakes;

sometimes there are rains of flowers and clouds of fragrance—all serve as catalysts for the teaching. Within this present sutra, there are two kinds of catalysts: first, the preaching of the sutra itself.
He entered meditative concentration, causing flowers to rain down and the earth to tremble, thereby acting as the remote catalyst.

Second, the dialogue between the two Great Beings regarding the light emitted from the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft of hair) acted as the proximate catalyst. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Now the Buddha emits a radiance to assist in the realization of the meaning of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)," and so forth.
The sixth [point] concerns the requester. This means that if one’s compassion is profound, one speaks spontaneously without being questioned, as the sūtra says:

"He spoke spontaneously without being asked," and so forth. However, if one holds the Dharma in high esteem and honors the person [of the teacher], and their sincerity and faith are deep, one must wait for an invitation before speaking;
as the sūtra says: "Since you have made three earnest requests, how could I not speak?"

Seventh, regarding the listeners: Those who preach the Dharma all rely upon individuals to be earnest. However, in accordance with the specific capacity of the audience, there are many reasons for doing so, primarily because the assembly requests instruction.
Thus, both the speaker and the requester act solely for the sake of the listeners, serving as a prologue and creating the necessary conditions.

Although it is said that conditions have their nearness and farness, and benefits their shallowness and depth, in reality, the afflictions of worldly toil and karmic delusions are ultimately liberated through this.
As the Sūtra says: "Even those who can hear but a single verse or a single phrase of this sūtra, I shall all bestow upon them the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thus we know that the prediction received today is truly a lingering trace of Jñānavijaya.
Furthermore, it must be understood that the remaining achievements of today are also the primary manifestations of future days.
Although these aforementioned causes and conditions vary in their degree of intimacy, they all possess the power to initiate the holy teaching.

By knowing the cause through its intimacy, one increases actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) and accomplishes one's own benefit. By knowing the superior capacity of assistance, one gives rise to expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
May the benefit of others be accomplished; may internal and external obstacles be pacified, so that one may forever behold the Buddha and hear the Dharma.

Regarding what is subsumed within the second treasury (the Sūtra-piṭaka), there are two parts: first, clarifying its inclusion within the treasuries, and second, clarifying its inclusion within the teachings. Within the first part, there are further two sections.

First the *piṭaka* (collections), then the *saṃgraha* (compendiums). To first clarify the *piṭaka*: it carries the sense of "containing" (*piṭaka*), because it is able to contain and gather that which is explained, preventing it from being dispersed.
Now, there are many types of *piṭakas*; to speak briefly, they are only two or three.

Regarding the two *piṭakas*, this refers to the World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings. Although their faculties are infinite, when summarized, they do not go beyond the Great [Vehicle]...

Because there are two vehicles—the Lesser Vehicle and the Great Vehicle—the compilers [of the canon] named them the "Lesser Vehicle Piṭaka" and the "Great Vehicle Piṭaka" based on the vehicle associated with the person.
As for what is called the "Three Piṭakas," the sacred teachings they elucidate do not exceed the Three Trainings. Thus, that which elucidates ethical discipline (*śīla*) is called the Vinaya Piṭaka;
that which elucidates meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is called the Sūtra Piṭaka; and that which elucidates the training in wisdom (*prajñā*) is called the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
Although each of these [categories] has its own primary and secondary aspects, the compilers followed the principle of "the few following the many" and assigned each to that which best expresses it.
Second, the explanation of subsumption also consists of two parts: first, the doctrine (*dharma*), and second, the ritual procedure (*vidhi*). Regarding the term "doctrine," it refers to all...
The various schools established their teachings differently, as detailed in the *Great Commentary* (*Dashu*).

For now, we take the five teachings established by the Great Master Xianshou as our primary authority, because their principles are most perfectly complete. These are the five: Hīnayāna (Small), Initial, Final, Sudden, and Perfect.
Their definitions, meanings, and purposes are also as recorded in the *Great Commentary*, so I shall not elaborate further here.
[The author] states: Next, to clarify what is subsumed [by this teaching]: this present sutra is able to fully exhaust the Tathāgata’s original intent for appearing in the world.

It correctly elucidates the ultimate, wondrous purport of the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao). Whether regarding doctrine or principle, practice or fruition, it completely discloses the innermost depths. As for the verbal teaching, it says:
"If one hears even a single verse or a single phrase of this sutra, all such persons shall be granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. Thus it is said.

Regarding principle (*li*), the phenomena of arising and ceasing in the world are, from the very moment they occur, eternally abiding. Regarding practice (*xing*), every movement—whether raising the head or lowering it—is a cause for attaining Buddhahood.

Regarding the fruit (*guo*), the eight difficulties are empty by nature, as evidenced by the Dragon Girl’s realization. Essentially, when one attains the principle and things are harmonized, all are in accord with reality;
this is the ultimate standard. If we discuss this in terms of its comprehensive application, such as when speaking of the "Small" [Vehicle]:

The emergence from the Truths (satya) is based on the "transformed city" (nirmita-nagara). To speak of "gradualism" (ji), one refers to Zhizhi, who clung to marks and harbored doubts regarding others.

To speak of "suddenness" (dun), one refers to the Dragon Girl, who entered realization. This directly abolishes all hierarchical stages. To speak of "perfection" (yuan), it is also like the Dragon Girl’s transformation of her appearance and swift realization;
yet, even within this perfect fusion, the sequential arrangement of practice is not discarded. Furthermore, it is said: "I possess immeasurable and boundless Buddha-wisdom."
In the "Joy of Wisdom" (Huìlè), the parable further states: "I possess such great seven-jeweled chariots, their number being immeasurable.
In both the Dharma and the parable, this is merely a brief indication of the principle of the primary and its attendants.
Regarding the second, the ritual procedures (*vidhi*): there are ten such procedures. Their enumeration and explanation are as judged in the Great Commentary (*Mahāṭīkā*).

To explain the ritual procedures for the present sutra, since they proceed from the small to the great, they are properly subsumed within the section on "Subsuming the Branches and Returning to the Root."

That which was thus spoken is for the purpose of refuting the notion of a multiplicity of vehicles (nānā-yāna). It also belongs to the gate of the non-obstruction between the fundamental and the derivative.

Furthermore, as in the *Devadatta-parivarta*, at that time, because the three and the one were in harmony, immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of Arhatship, and immeasurable sentient beings—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—realized the state of a Pratyekabuddha.
Sentient beings give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment, and so forth;

this is because the Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata is inconceivable and its provisional and ultimate aspects are unimpeded, thereby allowing those who hear it to receive its nourishment according to their respective capacities—whether they form three interpretations or take it as one. This is precisely the non-obstruction between the fundamental and the derivative, and between this and that.

Third, regarding the delimitation of the doctrinal principles (*arthaviniścaya*): it is already known that this sutra properly belongs to the final [vehicle], yet it also simultaneously elucidates the other four.
How is the scope within this [sutra] to be known? Now, when a single rain universally nourishes, all vehicles grow together.

When the sun’s orb reflects back, different paths return to the same destination. Thus, the fundamental and the derivative illuminate one another, and provisional and ultimate truths are bestowed together.
Within the Single Buddha Vehicle, three vehicles are distinguished and taught; yet though three are taught, they always serve a single purpose.

Although the gateways of meaning are immeasurable, they all arise from the subtle interplay of concealment and manifestation through this Dharma. Now, I shall offer my view through the narrow tube of limited perspective.

Reverently upholding the principles of the teachings, I shall propose three gates. First, "The Gate of Suddenly Revealing the Beginning and End," which unfolds the light to set the wheels in motion, consisting of questions and answers regarding the realm of wisdom.
Second, "The Gate of Causing One to Awaken to the Single Vehicle," which, relying on recent traces of manifestation, reveals the provisional to disclose the real.

Third, "The Gate of Causing Widespread Circulation," which relies on the fundamental fruit to manifest its virtues, sweeps away all traces to enter the profound mystery. Within the first of these, there are again two parts; the first...
I shall now draft a teaching net. Second, receiving the light, I shall present it in sequence. First, I shall draft a presentation of the Dharma of the transformer.

Although the scripture says, "each in their own world, they preach the True Dharma," and does not explicitly specify which dharma-gate this refers to, since the Way of all Buddhas is identical, we may take what was taught by our Buddha and apply it as a model for this. That is to say, regarding all Tathāgatas:

It should be like when our Buddha first attained perfect enlightenment: at that time and place, he spontaneously manifested an ocean of boundless sūtras—both explicit and implicit—flowing forth from his Brahma-like voice, which is free and sovereign in its expansion and contraction within a single locus where the vast and the narrow are non-obstructed and defilement and purity are mutually integrated;
and it should extensively reach all those who find it difficult [to understand], within a single moment where eons and thoughts are perfectly fused.
I reflect upon the assembly. However, within the Secret (Vajrayāna) division as well, there should likewise be distinctions among the five teachings; this is not what is being discussed here.
Now, regarding the Exoteric teachings, I shall briefly indicate two gates to demonstrate their various aspects: first, the gate of distinguishing characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vibhāga*);

second, the gate of comprehensive inclusion (*saṃgraha*). As for the gate of distinguishing characteristics: first, one takes the five teachings—Small, Initial, and so forth—as taught throughout the Tathāgata’s entire life. And...

Taken together, these constitute the Dharma-gate of the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), for they all flow from the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas—the great artistry that gathers in and delivers sentient beings.
Next, regarding the gradual opening according to increasing numbers: this refers to opening the Single Vehicle and dividing it into two.
This, in turn, has three aspects. First, distinguishing the Great from the Small: here, the former is the Small Vehicle, which is the teaching of the "half-letters" (*ardha-kṣara*).

The latter four are all Mahāyāna; that is, they constitute the teaching of the "full characters" (pūrṇākṣara). Second, when contrasting the provisional with the real, the first two—the Small Vehicle and the Initial [Vehicle]—are the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
The latter two—the Final, the Sudden, and the Perfect—are the teachings of the One Vehicle.

Third, although the Final and Sudden teachings sublate duality and differ from the former, they both contrast the three to reveal the one, thereby skillfully conforming to the capacities of sentient beings. The final [Perfect Teaching] directly reveals it.
This Dharma is called exclusively unshared (*āveṇika*). This is first categorized by the partial and the complete; second, by the provisional and the real; and third, by the crooked and the straight.

Each of these is divided into two, making three categories, or alternatively, they are divided into three. The first one is the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*); the second one is the Three Vehicles (*Triyāna*);
and the last one is the One Vehicle (*Ekayāna*). Alternatively, the last one is the unshared One Vehicle. If the first two are combined, then—
These are the three vehicles; the one vehicle (ekayāna) accords with the four vehicles. Accepting the judgment of Guangzhai, they may be divided into four. This further consists of two parts:
first, the three intermediate teachings, because the initial teaching (śāstric teaching) maintains the three [vehicles], while the final teaching (niṣṭhā-yāna) merges the two distinct [vehicles].
Thus, they are opened up into four: first, the distinct teaching of the Hīnayāna, such as the *Dīrgha Āgama* and others; second, the common teaching of the three vehicles.

1. The One Vehicle of Common Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-ekayāna*), such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and others; 2. The One Vehicle of Distinct Teaching (*viśeṣa-ekayāna*), such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and others.
Second, regarding the progression through stages (*krama*) and the absence of stages (*akrama*), which open up the gradual (*krama*) and the sudden (*tadakrama*), they are thus divided into four:

1. The Hīnayāna teaching; 2. The Gradual Teaching, referring to the beginning and the end; 3. The Sudden; 4. The Perfect. The above first classification is based on the meaning of existence and cessation (*sthiti-nirodha*).
There are four [divisions]. Second, regarding the classification by means of the sudden and gradual, these are further opened into four or five;

alternatively, they are divided into five, which corresponds to the teachings established by Master Zanghe. This is because, within the gradual teaching, the initial and final stages are distinguished, resulting in five.

Second is the "comprehensive inclusion" gate: this means that all three vehicles are, from the very beginning, the One Vehicle. Why is this so? If one considers the identity of the three and the one...
The two look toward each other and thus form two gates, namely: non-identity and non-difference. Question:
If those three and the one are not identical, it is unknown whether those three persist or perish. If they persist, how can there be only one?

If those capacities for the three vehicles were destroyed, upon what further dharma could they rely to continue their cultivation? The answer is: because there are four propositions. First, because they are identical [to the one], they do not depend on destruction.
Second, because they are identical [to the one], their persistence is not obstructed. Third, because they are identical [to the one], there is nothing that is not destroyed.
Fourth, because they are identical [to the one], there is nothing that can persist. By means of the first two propositions, those three...
By seizing the opportunity, one obtains that which serves as a basis. Through the latter two meanings, one enters into oneness.

Because these four phrases are simultaneously identical to one, there is thus only the One Vehicle (ekayāna) and no other vehicles. This is the comprehensive inclusion of the characteristics of the higher divisions.
"Dual yet non-dual. This is the meaning of the teaching that suddenly reveals the entire net of the Dharma. As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says:
"Cast the great net of the Teaching across the ocean of birth and death to scoop up the fish of humans and devas, and place them upon the shore of nirvāṇa. Furthermore, another sūtra states:
"With rain of a single flavor, it moistens the flowers of humanity, each of which attains its fruit. All these express this same intent. Above, within the light, he emulates the Tathāgata.
The various Dharma-gates that have been taught enable all bodhisattvas, upon hearing them, to possess various causes and conditions,
various modes of faith and understanding, and various characteristics as they practice the bodhisattva path; furthermore, those of the three vehicles are all subsumed within the One Vehicle,
thereby manifesting the premonitory signs for the teaching of the One Vehicle upon emerging from meditative concentration.

Regarding the manifestation of light for the sake of those of the Two Vehicles: this refers to those within the scope of the World-Honored One’s superior teaching-net who possess a distinct type of gradual-capacity.
Having already been disciplined and nurtured through various means until they reach the stage of maturity, they are now ready to hear the Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe.
For this reason, the World-Honored One first manifests rare and auspicious rays of light to awaken them.
This serves as the initial impetus, causing [beings] to give rise to longing and reverence, and furthering their aspiration for the sublime teachings.

Thus, within the initial response, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva fully sets forth matters such as the ancient Buddhas’ revelation of the Dharma, their bestowal of prophecies, and their entry into parinirvāṇa, thereby demonstrating that these are identical to what the present Buddha shall likewise do.
Consequently, what was the orthodox tradition of the past becomes the catalyst for the present day. Therefore, following the section on the fixed [teachings],...

There are matters such as "opening and revealing," none of which fall outside the scope of the answers to questions. Herein, I shall briefly indicate the principle of the perfect manifestation within the light;
there are three aspects: first, the direct demonstration of the fundamental light; second, the inclusion of the main teaching (*samyak-artha*);

and third, the extension into the dissemination (*pravartana*). Now, regarding the first, the direct demonstration: this refers to those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) who hold the sacred realm in high esteem while looking down upon [the ordinary].

One's own spirit takes the three realms as a perilous path; thus, for the sake of benefiting both self and others, the World-Honored One specifically manifested wondrous light from a single hair-pore, enabling one to realize that the boundless ocean of lands is not separate from the tip of a hair, and that the causes and effects of sages and ordinary beings do not transcend one’s own mind.
Furthermore, by receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, one is able to behold from afar various wonders.
Specifically, all of these exist in the present moment. Those who are deluded still claim that this is the supernatural power of the Buddha; how truly lamentable this is!

Second, regarding the inclusion of the orthodox teaching: it means that when pointing to the names that express [the meaning], one says, "At that time, the Buddha Sun Moon Lamp Brightness preached the Mahāyāna sūtra named the Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma," and furthermore, "By this, one knows the present Buddha."
When one intends to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, does it not accord perfectly with the name of the "Exalted *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*" that you should proclaim?
Regarding the meaning expressed by its characters, it says: "To expound the sūtras, which are subtle, wondrous, and foremost."
That voice is pure and emits a gentle sound. It then correctly addresses Śāriputra, saying:
"Hear the Buddha’s gentle voice, profound, far-reaching, and most subtle. It further says: "It can produce the foremost pure and wondrous bliss," and so forth. Furthermore, it says:

The Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment; the wondrous Dharma he attained was intended for this very teaching, or perhaps for the bestowal of a prediction of enlightenment—both of which already contain the essential purport of the orthodox doctrine. Third, regarding those passages that extend into the section on circulation:
this refers to such statements as, "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and expounded it for others for a full eighty minor kalpas."

Now, the propagation by the Bodhisattvas such as Bhaiṣajyarāja and others is precisely like the [exposition of the] marks of reality (lakṣaṇa). Thus we know that these three parts of this sutra are equally important;
it differs somewhat from other teachings for this specific reason. As for why they must be divided into three: it is so that one may know the beginning, middle, and end;
so that each has its own distinct manifestation; and because it is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end. Is this not the essence of a single sutra?
From beginning to end, do they not all remain inseparable from this single light? Question: How many kinds of light are there? Answer: There are two kinds.

The first is called the "constant light" (*nityaprabhā*). This arises from the Tathāgata’s entire body of diamond (*vajra*), which is transparently luminous both internally and externally, produced from that which is pure.
It is not necessary to emit it; thus, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, the World-Honored One possesses a constant radiance extending one fathom.
Second is the light that is emitted. If we infer by comparison with the present sutra, there should likewise be two kinds:
namely, first, the light of supernormal power (*ṛddhi-prabhā*), which all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emit whenever they seek to deliver sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured.
It enables those who behold it to extinguish their transgressions and increase their merit. It penetrates beyond all obstructions; though distant, it is as if near.
All its activities are contained within the first three realms. The light emitted by this present sutra may be called truly rare;
it differs greatly from that which is emitted in ordinary circumstances. Why is this? For all worldly...

World-Honored One, you have manifested within the five turbidities, and as your transformative conditions are nearing their end, you have now emitted this light, enabling one faculty to fully perceive the objects of all six faculties.
Regarding the objects thus attained, beings give rise to a sense of wonder and experience great joy, saying that they have obtained the objects of the six senses.
To see the destinations of birth and death is a realm attained by the divine eye; now, one sees them with the physical eye.
To perceive the karmic conditions of good and evil deeds is something attained through the knowledge of past lives; yet this too is attained by the physical eye.

To discern the various causes and conditions for seeking the Buddha-way, which belongs to the knowledge of others' minds, is likewise attained by the physical eye. It can cause that which is distant to become near.
This refers to the supernormal power of psychic travel (ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna). One attains it through the physical eye and hears the Dharma-gate of the Future Buddha (Upapadya-bodhisattva);

thus, one further advances toward the exhaustion of outflows (āsrava-kṣaya). Were it not for the addition of inconceivable divine wisdom within, one could not cause the assembly of all dharmas to gather.
By means of the illumination of a single light, does one eye-faculty simultaneously encompass the functions of the six supernormal powers and the three clarities?
Therefore, this is a rare and wondrous light.

Second, regarding the manifestation of transformation through proximate fruits, it reveals the provisional to disclose the real, causing those who realize the gateway of the One Vehicle [to do so]. As the sutra says:
When the Tathāgata was a prince, he departed from the palace of the Śākyas and sat at the site of enlightenment not far from there, attaining *bodhi*.
It has been no more than forty-odd years since then; this is the proximate fruit. Yet, for a certain class of gradual practitioners, he initially taught the One Vehicle.

The teaching of the three vehicles is established [as a provisional means]. Upon reaching the stage of maturation, one is once again gathered back into the three, which are then subsumed within the One Vehicle—this is what is meant by "opening and revealing" (*kaixian*).

However, if one wishes to understand the meaning of this opening and revealing, one must first master the principle that the provisional and the real are mutually fused and that the fundamental and the derivative are without obstruction;
otherwise, the provisional remains merely provisional and the fundamental remains merely fundamental. How then could there be any "opening and revealing"?
Now, this shall be briefly elucidated. The text has three parts: first, an explanation based on the Dharma, which directly reveals the One Vehicle;

second, an explanation based on metaphors, clarifying that originally there were no Three Vehicles; third, an explanation given for the purpose of cessation and provisionality, wherein the Three are shown.

Regarding the first two [of these], the first clarifies the mutual fusion of the provisional and the real, while the second correctly clarifies the revelation and manifestation. Now, concerning the initial fusion: within the aforementioned net of teachings, there is a certain kind...

This is for the purpose of implementing the provisional (*upāya*). From the fundamental source extending to its branches, the teachings—whether small or great, arranged in alternating sequence, or the layered accumulation of the *Hīnayāna* and *Mahāyāna*—all without exception lodge the real within the provisional to establish the Three Vehicles.

While this is equally easy to understand in the case of the *Hīnayāna*, within the *Mahāyāna* there are many kinds of distinctions. For instance, in the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, at times it is provisional...

In truth, both are clarified. At times, the provisional is employed to clarify the real; this is because, although the intent was originally to explain the real, the faculties [of the listeners] were still inferior.

At other times, the real is employed to clarify the provisional; this is because these [provisional teachings] descend from the one into the three, gradually leading [beings] to develop their faculties.

Furthermore, within the inconceivable Pure Name (Vimalakīrti), the provisional is refuted and the real is praised, so that through this permeation, their nature may be formed and they may be inspired to emulate it. Alas!
He reproached himself. Furthermore, the revelation in the Śrīmālā-sūtra somewhat resembles this present sutra;
it was intended to prevent those who were sitting still and not advancing from stagnating in the provisional, and it also served as a prologue for this present sutra.

These aforementioned dharma-gates all harmonize the Real within the Provisional, acting as a basis for guidance to break through their stagnation, so that when they reach Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, they may easily achieve integration.
If even one person were to receive this revelation and illumination, they would immediately realize that the three previous vehicles were in fact the one true vehicle.

Then, regarding the principle of non-identity and non-difference, it would become as clear as the melting of ice into water. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Within the single Buddha-vehicle, I have distinguished and taught three. It further states:
"Although I have spoken of the three vehicles, it is solely for the purpose of transforming bodhisattvas. In both cases, the real is integrated into the provisional.
This reconciles provisional means with ultimate reality. Furthermore, there is another category:

teachings that do not cling to expedient means, which profoundly clarify both nature (*xing*) and characteristics (*xiang*), and are equal in their intent, yet also serve as auxiliary conditions for drawing beings toward this sutra.

Moreover, there are those where both the beginning and end are Great, such as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*; and those where both the beginning and end are Small, such as the four Āgamas; all of these arise according to the awakening of sentient beings' capacities.
The extraordinary nature of its swift transcendence is such that it does not correspond at all with this [other] sutra; each is of a distinct category.

Second, the explicit clarification of the revelation: this means that within the essence of the present One Vehicle itself, there inherently exists a unique power to shatter differences, enabling the four factors of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit to each possess the meaning of revelation and so forth, standing in stark contrast to other sutras.

Therefore, the ancient commentaries summarize the principles of abolition, establishment, opening, and manifestation into the eight characters "convergence as the ultimate goal. Regarding the universal and the particular of this treatise, there are two meanings:

first, a general discussion of the universal and the particular; second, a definitive determination of what to discard and what to adopt. Within the initial general discussion, there are further two meanings: first, the universal followed by the particular.
As for the term "particular," it refers, for instance, to the meaning of abolition and establishment when viewed from the perspective of the Dharma-teachings.
Regarding the principle of "abolishing three and establishing one": this refers to viewing the present sutra from the perspective of the external, provisional teachings of former times.
There exists a specific intent to abolish those three former [vehicles] and separately establish the principle of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) of the present day.
This is because the three vehicles of the past possess only provisional names; as the sutra says: "But by means of provisional names, I guide sentient beings. It further states: "The world..."
After a long time, the Honored One must speak the truth; therefore, this teaching itself contains two meanings.

First, there is the meaning of being definitively subject to abolition, and thus it is now abolished. Second, there is the meaning of the expressive words serving as the cause, which cannot be abolished;

therefore, the subsequent text includes this within the four meanings subsumed under the character "open" (*kāi*). Second, regarding the meaning of "opening and revealing," in relation to the principle (*li*),...
Regarding Fazang’s clarification of "opening the three to reveal the one": this means that if one speaks of there being three, then the principle of the ultimate One naturally remains hidden;
if one opens up the principle that there are no three, then the ultimate One naturally manifests. To "converge the three" is the meaning.
Regarding Fazang’s clarification of "converging the three into one" in terms of practice: this means that practices in the past each tended toward their own respective fruits, whereas now...

They are harmonized as being equally causes for Buddhahood. If even raising a hand or bowing the head can serve as a cause for Buddhahood, how much more so the Truths (*satya*), the Conditions (*pratyaya*), and the Perfections (*pāramitā*)?
Regarding the meaning of the fourfold convergence and return: looking toward the fruit-dharma, it clarifies that the three refuges are unified into one.

This means that the fruits obtained by the Three Vehicles through the severance of delusions are merely states of samādhi; now, they are harmonized and integrated so that all return to the One Vehicle. And...

It serves as the cause for the ultimate fruit. Furthermore, regarding the principle of "abolishing" (*fei*), if one considers it in relation to the dharma that constitutes the fruit, there are also two senses.

First, if it refers to the provisional establishment of the characteristics of the fruit, then it may be abolished. Second, if it refers to the sublation of the fruit to serve as the cause, then it cannot be abolished.

Here, the latter sense is employed: the provisional fruit is sublated to become the cause of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Next, regarding what is called "universal" (*tong*), only one type is abolished.

This then concludes the section on the teaching. Regarding the opening and manifestation [of the truth] as its ultimate convergence, these apply equally to all four types of teachings, beginning with the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).

Now, first, let us clarify how the character "opening" (*kai*) applies to these four. In terms of the teaching itself, previously the three vehicles were taught for the sake of the three types of practitioners;
now it is said that there are neither two nor three. Previously, the claim that there are three was a provisional gate that closed off the single reality; now, that [closure] is no more.
When two or three [vehicles] are established, the One Vehicle manifests of itself; therefore it is said that this sutra opens the gate of expedient means and reveals the true aspect.

This refers to the superior [truth], wherein the causal, expressive language cannot be discarded, thereby clarifying what is meant by "opening. It is through the language of worldly convention (*saṃvṛti-satya*) [that this is expressed].

One does not even turn one's back upon the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), let alone the teachings of the Three Vehicles. If we speak in terms of principle, previously three principles were taught, meaning they were realized individually;

now it is shown that the *dharmakāya* is identical, with no further distinct flavors. Previously, by saying there are three, the door of skillful means (*upāyamukha*) was closed regarding the single reality;
now, by saying there are not three, the single principle manifests of itself, thereby opening up the square [of the ultimate].

This is the "Gate of Expedient Means" (*upāyamukha*), which reveals the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). If we consider the practitioner: previously, it was taught that the practices of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) were each distinct;
